1.pericope_label: Who did sin, this man or his parents? I must work the works of him that sent me

schools.summary: Robertson settles the text at “we must work the works of him that sent me”, joining the disciples to Christ’s commission and dismissing Bernard’s defence of the singular; Ellicott reads the disciples’ question as a mystery of life brought in all its darkness rather than a subject for debate, and warns that its form leaves both alternatives open; Lightfoot dismantles transmigration on Josephus’s own terms; Barnes makes the night death.

Calvin names three errors in judging the afflicted — censuring others while sparing ourselves, reading any stroke as deadly hatred, and condemning all whom God visits, when Job was more wretched than any man not for sin but that his piety might be proved — and answers the objection that God’s power shone brighter after Christ’s death by making the bodily presence the true day whose lustre reaches every age.

Clarke surveys transmigration through Pythagoras, Josephus, Philo and a Hindu schedule of punishments, and concludes the blindness fell in the ordinary course of providence; Wesley presses that no man can work toward his salvation once this life is ended, though Christ can work always.

Henry finds it noble and Christ-like to serve a public that has slighted us, and warns that we make more haste than good speed when we outrun opportunities of doing good; he also cautions against accusing those whom God has justified.

Chrysostom makes the exit from the temple deliberate, so that absence might cool their fury and the miracle soften them, notes that Christ saw the man and not the man Christ, and refuses to allow that the blindness was unjust, since it brought him to see with the inward eye; Theophylact finds the disciples’ question improper and hard to account for.

Augustine holds that both the man and his parents had sinned, though that sin was not the cause of his blindness, and that beyond the night is neither faith nor labour nor repentance, while the day of Christ’s presence lasts to the end of the world; Bede reads the passing by as the descent from heaven.

debates.question: Whose sin, if any, lay behind the blindness?

positions.view: Neither, as the question is bounded — the affliction fell in the ordinary course of providence
Both had sinned, but that sin was not the cause of this blindness
The blindness was itself a benefit, bringing him to inward sight

outliers.claim: Refutes transmigration from Josephus: only good souls were held to pass into other bodies, so unless one will say a good man’s soul produced this blindness, the principle says nothing to the case.

themes: And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth.
And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?
Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.
I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.

6.pericope_label: He made clay of the spittle: go, wash in the pool of Siloam

schools.summary: Robertson cites Dods against any virtue in the clay, since Christ used none in other cures; Ellicott takes the opposite view and lets the means be means, citing Pliny, Tacitus and Suetonius on fasting saliva as a recognised eye remedy, and records the reading, as old as Irenaeus, that the clay recalls the creation of man from dust; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic tale behind the sabbath prohibition; Barnes builds the deliberate offence into a lesson on their keeping of the day.

Calvin makes the sending to Siloam a trial of faith, the cure beginning so absurdly that it seems to double the blindness, yet the man goes on a bare word, his faith the more commendable for resting on so small a knowledge.

Clarke doubts any medical tendency and concludes God works in his own way, hiding pride from man by means contrary to the end proposed; Wesley presses that the treatment might almost have blinded a man who could see.

Chrysostom explains the spittle rather than water so that nothing be ascribed to the fountain, and the delay before washing so that the Jews’ obstinacy might be overcome by the sight of him walking with clay on his eyes, no glory accruing to a pool where many had washed without benefit.
Augustine reads the sequence sacramentally, the man anointed but not yet seeing as one made a catechumen, enlightened only when sent and washed.

debates.question: Does the name Siloam point to the Shiloh of Jacob’s blessing?

positions.view: Yes, the fountain typifying the Sent of God
No — the words come from different roots, and there is no evidence John had the prophecy in mind
The gloss distinguishes the upper pool Siloah from the lower Shelah

outliers.claim: Publicly withdraws the identification of Siloam with Shiloh that he had printed in his own first edition, on the ground that the two words come from different roots.

themes: When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay,
And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing.

8.pericope_label: Is not this he that sat and begged? A man that is called Jesus made clay

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the reading from “saw he was blind” to “saw he was a beggar”, and finds in the whole scene the form natural to a narrative taken from an eyewitness, possibly the man himself; Robertson notes his regular pitch as a familiar figure; Lightfoot and Clarke give the formulas Jewish beggars used, which were offers rather than requests.

Calvin observes that impiety is ingenious in obscuring God’s works, so the brighter the display the less credit it wins, yet the doubting served the miracle by drawing a fuller testimony from the man.
Clarke calls the man’s account simple and artless in the highest degree, noting he says only that clay was made, not that it was made of spittle, since he could not see the spitting.

Henry reads it as providence that the subject was a common beggar and therefore widely known, so the miracle was better attested; he finds a lesson in the posture — if we cannot work for God we must sit still quietly for him — and makes the reporting of mercies a duty, since God’s favours are lost upon us when they go no further.

Chrysostom turns the poverty into an argument, that God heals even beggars and chooses the meanest so as to stop his critics’ mouths, marks the exactness of the man’s account, and judges the question where is he to have come from men already meditating Christ’s death.

Augustine says the opened eyes had altered his look, hears gratitude in the two words I am he, and makes him one anointed but not yet seeing, who preaches and knows not what he preaches; Bede makes him the catechumen, believing but not yet washed.

debates.question: Why did Christ withdraw immediately after the cure?

positions.view: So that no suspicion might attach to the miracle, the healed man having no chance to publish a false cure to oblige him
So that in the work of grace we should see the change without the hand that makes it

outliers.claim: Records the beggars’ own formulas — deserve something by me, do yourselves good by me, and, for those come down in the world, look back and see what I have been.

themes: The neighbours therefore, and they which before had seen him that he was blind, said, Is not this he that sat and begged?
Some said, This is he: others said, He is like him: but he said, I am he.
Therefore said they unto him, How were thine eyes opened?
He answered and said, A man that is called Jesus made clay, and anointed mine eyes, and said unto me, Go to the pool of Siloam, and wash: and I went and washed, and I received sight.
Then said they unto him, Where is he? He said, I know not.

13.pericope_label: It was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay: he is a prophet

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the day at the last great day of the feast and names the two offences, kneading clay and anointing eyes with spittle, no healing being allowed except in immediate danger; Robertson says this mattered to them more than whether the thing was done; Barnes turns their procedure into a lasting reproach, that the proper question was whether it had happened, not how; Lightfoot explains that John’s Pharisees generally mean the Sanhedrin.

Calvin says they leave the fact aside and argue only the law, assuming an error refuted a hundred times, and warns that the argument from miracles is not conclusive by itself, since Satan counterfeits God’s works like an ape.
Clarke holds that magicians might do things apparently miraculous but nothing really good, and would safely defy all Egypt’s magicians to open one blind man’s eyes.

Henry gives three reasons why Christ healed on that day and in a manner certain to offend — he would not yield to a usurped authority whose zeal for rituals had consumed the substance of religion, he meant to expound the fourth commandment and clear it of their glosses, and he chose the day to dignify it.

Chrysostom notes they pass over the miracle to press the supposed transgression, and that none dared say openly what he thought; in the homilies he infers from the new form of the question that the speakers are the seceding party; Theophylact reads the same good intent in it.

Augustine observes it was some and not all, since some were already anointed, and turns the charge round — to keep the sabbath spiritually is to have no sin, so they kept it carnally and transgressed it spiritually; he also allows that they may have sought a handle to cast the man out.

debates.question: Do miracles by themselves prove a divine mission?

positions.view: Yes — no sinner could do such signs, and the early opponents never denied the facts
Not by themselves, since God permits false prophets some wonders and Satan counterfeits his works

outliers.claim: Cites Suetonius on the blind man at Alexandria whose eyes Vespasian opened with spittle at the direction of Serapis in a dream, asking who would reckon Vespasian among the servants of God, and ascribing the case to a righteous vengeance on those who despise true miracles.

themes: They brought to the Pharisees him that aforetime was blind.
And it was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and opened his eyes.
Then again the Pharisees also asked him how he had received his sight. He said unto them, He put clay upon mine eyes, and I washed, and do see.

Therefore said some of the Pharisees, This man is not of God, because he keepeth not the sabbath day. Others said, How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles? And there was a division among them.
They say unto the blind man again, What sayest thou of him, that he hath opened thine eyes? He said, He is a prophet.

18.pericope_label: They called the parents: he is of age, ask him, for they feared the Jews

schools.summary: Ellicott says they hoped fear would draw from the parents a denial of either the identity or the congenital blindness; Robertson calls the compound question shrewd and says plainly they summoned the parents to cover their own stupidity, the two admissions then cutting the ground from under the denial; Barnes sets out the two grades of Jewish excommunication and judges it was dread of the heavier that silenced them.

Calvin holds their unbelief voluntary, nothing hindering them from seeing an obvious work of God but the malice that keeps the eyes shut, and finds in the multiplied questions a design to prevent any reply.

Henry turns the parents’ frank avowal into a reproof of those ashamed of a child’s infirmity, judges their evasion cowardly since in a day of trial the man not apparently for Christ is reckoned against him, and finds in the phrase they hid behind a rule about children speaking for themselves once of age; he closes on the contrast that the simple-hearted poor draw the proper inference while others are ever learning and never come to the knowledge of the truth.

Chrysostom says it is the nature of truth to be strengthened by the snares laid against it, notes that producing the parents cuts off the plea of mere resemblance, and asks what gratitude conceals what it knows from fear; Theophylact sets out the dilemma they intended and contrasts the fainthearted parents with their intrepid son.

Augustine glosses the referral wittily, that we might justly be compelled to speak for an infant who cannot speak, but this man was never dumb, and dismisses the threat in a sentence — whom they cast out, Christ took in; Alcuin notes the Evangelist is careful to show the answer came from fear and not ignorance.

debates.question: Was calling the parents a wise move?

positions.view: Self-defeating, since it removed the plea of resemblance and threw the case on the man’s own confession
A calculated attempt to use fear to obtain a denial

outliers.claim: Details the heavier excommunication, called the curse, which excluded a man perpetually with maledictions and forbade anyone to sell him even the necessaries of life.

themes: But the Jews did not believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and received his sight, until they called the parents of him that had received his sight.
And they asked them, saying, Is this your son, who ye say was born blind? how then doth he now see?
His parents answered them and said, We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind:
But by what means he now seeth, we know not; or who hath opened his eyes, we know not: he is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself.
These words spake his parents, because they feared the Jews: for the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.
Therefore said his parents, He is of age; ask him.

24.pericope_label: Give God the praise: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see

schools.summary: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree that give glory to God is an adjuration, the words Joshua used to Achan, and not a call to gratitude — Ellicott adding that the common reading is impossible since they assume no cure occurred, and Robertson that they wished to settle a question of fact by authority, as persecutors have in every age; Ellicott also shows how one thing marks the chief matter to the exclusion of all else.

Calvin exposes the double move, a plausible exhortation to honour God followed by a prohibition against answering according to conviction, and turns aside to the oath itself, since men who forget they deny God when they invoke him to uphold a falsehood have filled every place with perjuries.
Clarke notes they put the man on his solemn oath while trying to put their own words in his mouth.

Henry makes the man’s one certainty the pattern of testimony, since we may take the comfort of a change whose steps we cannot trace if we can say that whereas I was blind, now I see, and adds that the unbelief of those who enjoy every means of conviction is the thing truly to be marvelled at.

Chrysostom explains the guarded reply as judgment and not fear, the defence lying better in the fact than in the man’s own pleading, and generalises that truth is strength and falsehood weakness, so truth ennobles whomever it takes up however mean before.

Augustine says denying the benefit received is not to give God glory but to blaspheme him, reads the retort as it stands — I am his disciple already, do you wish to be? — and refuses to let the abuse stand as abuse, since thou art his disciple is a curse only in the speakers’ intention; Alcuin says the man answered so as neither to invite calumny nor conceal the truth, and marks how his tone hardened once the victory was won.

debates.question: Why does the man say he does not know whether Christ is a sinner, having called him a prophet?

positions.view: Judgment rather than fear — the fact was a stronger defence than his own pleading
Irony, meant to wound them the more deeply

outliers.claim: Compares the repeated questioning to hounds following wherever the scent takes them, and notes they ask not how he came to see but how his eyes were opened, hoping he might detract from the operation.

themes: Then again called they the man that was blind, and said unto him, Give God the praise: we know that this man is a sinner.
He answered and said, Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
Then said they to him again, What did he to thee? how opened he thine eyes?
He answered them, I have told you already, and ye did not hear: wherefore would ye hear it again? will ye also be his disciples?
Then they reviled him, and said, Thou art his disciple; but we are Moses’ disciples.
We know that God spake unto Moses: as for this fellow, we know not from whence he is.

30.pericope_label: Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one born blind

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers the reading the marvellous thing, hears the sting in the pronoun addressed to men whose business it was to know, lays the man’s argument out as a syllogism, and warns that the premise has been lifted from its context to bear a darkness it cannot carry; Robertson finds him angry at last and says he has scored with terrific power in his use of Scripture and logic; Barnes hedges the premise with qualifications, denying it any bearing on the prayers sinners make for salvation.

Calvin refuses the softening: those who think the man merely echoed popular opinion are mistaken, since it is the uniform doctrine of Scripture that God listens to none but such as call on him in truth, the prayer of the wicked being an abomination.

Clarke offers a middle course, taking the word for heathen — those not proselyted, set against a worshipper of the true God — and joins Barnes in reporting that sight was never restored to one born blind by natural means until Cheselden couched a young man’s eyes in 1728; Wesley limits the saying to the impenitent and marvels that a man utterly illiterate should argue with such strength and clearness.

Chrysostom observes that so long as they expected a denial they were willing to believe him, and that in making his blindness the fruit of his sins they reason most unreasonably; in the homilies he turns the expulsion into a promise, the Jews casting him out of the Temple and the Lord of the Temple finding him.

Augustine notes the ingratitude precisely, that they had made him their teacher by questioning him so often and now expel him for teaching, and reads altogether to mean he was wholly blind, yet he who opened his eyes saves him altogether too.

debates.question: In what sense does God not hear sinners?

positions.view: An uninspired man’s opinion, with no bearing on prayers for salvation
True as Scripture teaches it — God hears none but those who call on him in truth
The word means heathen, or the impenitent, not sinners as such

outliers.claim: Answers the modern objection in advance: that surgery can now cure congenital blindness is beside the question, unless it is pretended human skill could do it under the same conditions and by the same means.

themes: The man answered and said unto them, Why herein is a marvellous thing, that ye know not from whence he is, and yet he hath opened mine eyes.
Now we know that God heareth not sinners: but if any man be a worshipper of God, and doeth his will, him he heareth.
Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind.
If this man were not of God, he could do nothing.
They answered and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out.

35.pericope_label: Dost thou believe on the Son of God? Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him

schools.summary: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree that the word rendered Lord here means no more than Sir, the ordinary address to a prophet or teacher.
Calvin cautions that what the man reaches at this point is a very small and cold portion of faith, a beginning from which Christ meant to lead him further.

Henry makes it a rule that earthly princes cannot notice everyone who defends them while Christ observes every faithful testimony, and that persecutors who shut a good man out of their communion cannot shut him out of communion with Christ; he finds the chief comfort of bodily sight in its usefulness to faith, notes that Christ revealed himself so plainly to almost no one else, and observes that the man was asking where the Saviour was at the moment he spoke with him.

Chrysostom makes the finding deliberate, Christ receiving the man as a judge receives the wrestler after his labours, and reads his counter-question as the speech of a longing mind that does not yet know the one for whom it has contended; Theophylact hears in thou hast seen him a reminder of the cure, and adds a caution against Nestorius.

Augustine marks the sequence, the face of the heart washed first and the Son of God then acknowledged, and says that I believe is a small thing beside the falling down and worshipping; Bede takes the posture for a lesson in prayer; Hilary presses the exact form of the question, that faith is asked not for Christ, a name heretics have readily in their mouths, but for the Son of God, and not for a Son who is a creature.

debates.question: Did the man already know who had healed him?

positions.view: No — he was blind before the cure and seized immediately after, so had never seen his benefactor
He knew the voice and half expected this speaker to be the Messiah himself

outliers.claim: Insists the question is framed as the Son of God and not as Christ, since heretics confess Christ while denying the Son, and that believing on the Son as a creature profits nothing.

themes: Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him, he said unto him, Dost thou believe on the Son of God?
He answered and said, Who is he, Lord, that I might believe on him?
And Jesus said unto him, Thou hast both seen him, and it is he that talketh with thee.
And he said, Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him.

39.pericope_label: For judgment I am come into this world: if ye were blind, ye should have no sin

schools.summary: Barnes denies that judgment can mean condemnation, since Christ elsewhere disclaims coming to condemn, and reads the effect rather than the design; Ellicott notes the word John uses only here means the sentence pronounced rather than the act of judging, so that the light judged no man and yet by it every man was judged, and insists both phrases are read from the speakers’ own point of view.
Gill finds the doubling in the word itself, a judgment inflicting judicial blindness on some while in mercy illuminating others.
Clarke states it flatly, that salvation is taken from those who reject it and the kingdom given to the Gentiles.

Henry applies the saying to nations and then to persons, catches what stung in the Pharisees’ retort — the rabbis, the doctors, the learned in the law — and remarks that those who most need reproof have wit enough to detect a tacit one and not grace enough to bear a just one; he presses the medical figure, that no patients are so hard to manage as those in a frenzy who say nothing ails them.

Chrysostom distinguishes a twofold sight and a twofold blindness, of sense and of understanding, these men being ashamed only of the first, and reaches for Paul’s formulation about the Gentiles who attained a righteousness Israel missed; Theophylact allows that ignorance of the Scriptures would have made the offence lighter.

Augustine identifies the judgment as this act of division and not the judgment of the last day, and states the diagnosis plainly: if you called yourselves blind and ran to the physician you would have no sin, but saying we see, you seek no physician and remain in your blindness.

debates.question: What kind of judgment is meant?

positions.view: The sentence men pronounce on themselves by accepting or rejecting the light
Not a design but an effect, some being reformed and some hardened
A judicial blinding of some alongside the illumination of others

outliers.claim: Calls the Pharisees’ protest a libel on the great, and holds that nothing fortifies a corrupt heart against the word so effectually as the high opinion others have of it.

themes: And Jesus said, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.
And some of the Pharisees which were with him heard these words, and said unto him, Are we blind also?
Jesus said unto them, If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.
